classification.difficultyReason: Construct a parallelogram using corresponding angles, justify parallel sides and verify side and diagonal properties by measurement.

questions.mappingNote: The main assessed content is verification of parallelogram side and diagonal properties; construction and parallel-line reasoning support that task. The opening solution panel on page 5 belongs to Example 2 and is excluded teaching evidence.
questions.methodNote: Use protractor construction and equal corresponding angles to establish opposite parallel sides. Verify opposite-side equality and diagonal bisection by ruler measurements on the student's construction.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct a parallelogram using corresponding angles, justify parallel sides and verify side and diagonal properties by measurement.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the equal opposite sides property directly to two given side lengths.

questions.mappingNote: This question directly assesses the opposite-side property with no algebra or congruence proof required.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 proves that opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal. Pages 4–5 summarise this property and use it to identify missing side lengths, naming the parallelogram in the reason.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the equal opposite sides property directly to two given side lengths.

classification.difficultyReason: Reproduce the taught proof of both pairs of equal opposite angles using supplementary co-interior angles.

questions.mappingNote: The assessed task is a proof of a parallelogram property from its parallel-side definition, making prove-properties-triangles-quadrilaterals the closest catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 proves opposite angles equal by applying supplementary co-interior angles successively and substituting. Apply that same method with the question's vertex names; do not assume the property being proved.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Reproduce the taught proof of both pairs of equal opposite angles using supplementary co-interior angles.

classification.difficultyReason: Adapt the explicitly referenced taught proof: identify two alternate-angle equalities and equal opposite sides, establish triangle congruence, then infer equality of the matching diagonal segments.

questions.mappingNote: The task asks for a proof of diagonal bisection, so citing diagonal bisection alone would be circular. The directly assessed skill is proving a quadrilateral property through triangle congruence.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 proves diagonal bisection using two alternate-angle equalities, equality of opposite sides, AAS congruence and matching sides. The solution follows that sequence with the question's vertex names.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Adapt the explicitly referenced taught proof: identify two alternate-angle equalities and equal opposite sides, establish triangle congruence, then infer equality of the matching diagonal segments.

classification.difficultyReason: Select explicitly taught opposite-angle/side/diagonal properties across six figures, combine a reflex-angle subtraction and solve three simple linear equations; all representations and targets are supplied.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and c apply angle properties; b applies opposite sides and bisected diagonals; d combines opposite angles with the angle sum at a point; e uses supplementary co-interior angles; f turns bisected diagonals and equal opposite sides into linear equations. The supplied reuse candidates have different original tasks and are ineligible.
questions.methodNote: Use equal opposite angles, equal opposite sides and bisected diagonals, proved on page 3 and summarised on page 4. Example 1 on page 4 models named parallelograms, straight and vertically opposite angles, and co-interior angle equations. The continuation of Example 2 on page 5 models equal-side and angle reasoning.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select parallelogram properties, identify a reflex angle and solve linear equations arising from bisected diagonals and equal opposite sides.

classification.difficultyReason: Four direct perimeter calculations using the stated parallelogram property, including one familiar half-unit length; no modelling choice or proof.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts directly apply Example 2's perimeter method to two supplied side lengths. The most advanced directly assessed skill is calculating perimeter; no congruence proof or angle calculation is requested.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 states and proves that opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal. Example 2 on pages 4–5 obtains the two missing side lengths using that property, then adds all four lengths to calculate perimeter.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Directly apply equal opposite sides and add four lengths, including decimal and mixed-number lengths.

classification.difficultyReason: Follow a specified construction and explain two circle intersections using diagonal bisection.

questions.mappingNote: Question 7 applies diagonal bisection to circles centred at the diagonal intersection: equal distances from M establish that opposite endpoints lie on the same circle. The construction is prescribed; no formal congruence proof is requested.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 defines parallelograms and investigates their diagonals. Page 3 proves diagonal bisection using AAS congruence, and page 4 summarises the property. Page 5 Exercise 13A question 1 supplies a construction and asks students to check that the diagonal intersection is the midpoint of each diagonal.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Follow a specified construction and explain two circle intersections using diagonal bisection.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the explicitly taught diagonal-bisection property to two symbolic half-lengths, double both and compare their ratio; no new proof selection is demanded.

questions.mappingNote: Use diagonal bisection in ABCD to double AM=2x and BM=x, then compare the complete diagonals. The task applies a proved property; it does not require a fresh congruence proof.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 proves that the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other. Page 4 summarises this property and instructs students to name the particular parallelogram when using its properties.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply diagonal bisection to two labelled half-diagonals and establish the ratio of the complete diagonals.

classification.difficultyReason: The two-part scaffold supplies the intermediate angle result and directs its use. Students combine the quadrilateral angle sum with the converse co-interior angle property twice to prove the defining parallel-side conditions.

questions.mappingNote: The question explicitly scaffolds the converse proof: establish supplementary adjacent angles, then use the converse co-interior angle property to prove both pairs of opposite sides parallel. No congruence argument is needed.
questions.methodNote: Page 1 states the quadrilateral angle sum. Page 2 defines a parallelogram by opposite parallel sides. Page 3 proves the opposite-angle property using co-interior angles. Pages 4–5 model angle reasoning with stated geometric reasons, and page 5 identifies the converse properties as exercise proofs.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: The two-part scaffold supplies the intermediate angle result and directs its use. Students combine the quadrilateral angle sum with the converse co-interior angle property twice to prove the defining parallel-side conditions.

classification.difficultyReason: Prove the opposite-sides test for a parallelogram using SSS congruence and the converse of the alternate-angle property.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed result is the opposite-sides test for a parallelogram; congruent-triangle proof and parallel-line angle reasoning support that result.
questions.methodNote: Use the side-angle-side correspondence style of the geometric proofs on page 3, here establishing SSS from the given opposite-side equalities and common diagonal. Use matching angles and the converse alternate-angle property, then the definition of a parallelogram on page 2. Page 5 explicitly identifies converse properties as exercise proofs.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Prove the opposite-sides test for a parallelogram using SSS congruence and the converse of the alternate-angle property.

classification.difficultyReason: Follow explicit ruler/compass construction, connect the constructed radii to equal opposite sides, then verify angles by measurement; the method and checks are supplied.

questions.mappingNote: The principal reasoning is applying the equal-opposite-sides test to justify a compass construction; angle measurement is a supporting check.
questions.methodNote: Use compass radii to obtain equal opposite sides and apply the parallelogram test stated immediately after question 10 on page 8. Check opposite angles by protractor, consistent with the property proved on page 3.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct a quadrilateral using compass radii, justify it using equal opposite sides, and check opposite angles by measurement.

classification.difficultyReason: Use equal opposite angles to equate their bisected halves, then transfer an angle using parallel sides and recognise corresponding angles to prove the bisectors parallel; the diagram supplies the half-angle labels but leaves this proof connection unstated.

questions.mappingNote: This question proves a relationship between angle bisectors using the established opposite-angle property and the converse corresponding-angle property; it does not require congruent triangles.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 defines a parallelogram by opposite parallel sides. Page 3 proves equality of opposite angles using parallel-line angle properties. Pages 4–5 model naming the property used at each step.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use equal opposite angles to equate their bisected halves, then transfer an angle using parallel sides and recognise corresponding angles to prove the bisectors parallel; the diagram supplies the half-angle labels but leaves this proof connection unstated.

classification.difficultyReason: Establish two triangle congruences and use the opposite-sides test to prove that an internal quadrilateral is a parallelogram.

questions.mappingNote: The final assessed task is proving a quadrilateral satisfies a parallelogram test; formal triangle congruence is the supporting method.
questions.methodNote: Use opposite sides of a parallelogram, alternate angles and SAS congruence to establish equal opposite sides of PBQD. Apply the opposite-sides test proved in question 10 on page 8.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Establish two triangle congruences and use the opposite-sides test to prove that an internal quadrilateral is a parallelogram.

classification.difficultyReason: Follow a compass construction and justify four equal sides using equal radii.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed property is equality of all four rhombus sides. The supplied construction establishes these equalities from the common compass radius.
questions.methodNote: Page 9 defines a rhombus by its four equal sides. Question 1 supplies its own equal-radius circle construction; the justification uses radii and that definition, without requiring diagonal properties.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Follow a compass construction and justify four equal sides using equal radii.

classification.difficultyReason: Reproduce the demonstrated diagonal angle-bisection proof with relabelled vertices, choosing matching SSS triangles and stating the corresponding angle consequence.

questions.mappingNote: Question 3 asks for that same proof with vertices relabelled X, Y, Z and W. The proof establishes the property from equal sides rather than citing the property being proved.
questions.methodNote: Page 10 proves angle bisection by comparing the triangles on either side of a rhombus diagonal using SSS, then using matching angles of congruent triangles.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Reproduce the taught SSS proof that a rhombus diagonal bisects a vertex angle.

classification.difficultyReason: Adapt the explicitly referenced earlier proofs: use alternate angles and equal sides for diagonal bisection, then connect SSS angle bisection, isosceles base angles and triangle angle sums to establish perpendicularity. The taught proof route supplies the essential connections.

questions.mappingNote: The question explicitly asks for the earlier proof with vertices PQRS. The solution reproduces those methods with the corresponding vertex names, rather than assuming the property being proved.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 proves diagonal bisection using alternate angles and AAS. Page 9 establishes that a rhombus is a parallelogram. Page 10 proves angle bisection using SSS and perpendicularity using isosceles base angles and triangle angle sums.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Adapt the explicitly referenced earlier proofs: use alternate angles and equal sides for diagonal bisection, then connect SSS angle bisection, isosceles base angles and triangle angle sums to establish perpendicularity. The taught proof route supplies the essential connections.

classification.difficultyReason: Follow the explicit protractor/compass construction, justify rhombus equality from adjacent equal sides and parallel pairs, then check diagonal bisection/perpendicularity; the construction and measurement tasks are scaffolded.

questions.mappingNote: The task directly applies the rhombus definition on page 9 and diagonal properties on page 10, using the ruler, compass and protractor construction approach illustrated in Exercise 13B on page 11.
questions.methodNote: Use corresponding angles to establish parallel sides, equal radii to establish adjacent equal sides, and opposite-side equality in a parallelogram. Check the rhombus diagonal properties by protractor measurement as requested.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Follow four supplied construction steps, connect corresponding angles and equal compass radii to a parallelogram with equal adjacent sides, then verify the stated diagonal properties by measurement.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct a rectangle and its circumcircle, explaining the construction using equal diagonals that bisect each other.

questions.mappingNote: The assessed explanation directly applies rectangle diagonal properties to a construction; quadrilateral-properties is the closest supplied catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Pages 2–3 introduce diagonal properties and prove that parallelogram diagonals bisect each other. Page 14 states and proves that rectangle diagonals are equal and bisect each other. Page 15 applies these properties to equal half-diagonals. Page 16 explicitly explains the circumcircle centred at their intersection.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct a rectangle and its circumcircle, explaining the construction using equal diagonals that bisect each other.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct a square accurately, verify its diagonal angles and explain its circumcircle using diagonal properties.

questions.mappingNote: The assessed task is an accurate compass-and-line construction followed by verification and explanation of square properties. Quadrilateral properties is the closest primary skill; the protractor skills cover the perpendicular construction and requested measurements.
questions.methodNote: Pages 2–3 establish quadrilateral definitions and parallelogram angle and diagonal properties. Pages 9–10 establish that a rhombus is a parallelogram and its diagonals are perpendicular angle bisectors. Pages 14–15 give rectangle and square definitions and equal, bisecting diagonals. Page 16 explicitly explains the circumcircle through the four vertices using equal diagonals and their common midpoint.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct a square accurately, verify its diagonal angles and explain its circumcircle using diagonal properties.

classification.difficultyReason: Use supplementary co-interior angles to establish four right angles and apply the definition of a rectangle.

questions.mappingNote: The task requires a proof of a quadrilateral property using parallel-line angle reasoning and the rectangle definition.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 defines a parallelogram by its parallel opposite sides. Page 3 uses supplementary co-interior angles to prove angle properties. Page 14 defines a rectangle as a quadrilateral with four right angles.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use supplementary co-interior angles to establish four right angles and apply the definition of a rectangle.

classification.difficultyReason: For the explicitly named triangles, select equal opposite sides, the common side and included right angles to establish SAS congruence, then use corresponding sides to conclude that the diagonals are equal.

questions.mappingNote: The assessed task is a proof of a rectangle property through congruent triangles. The quadrilateral-property proof skill is primary, with formal triangle congruence secondary.
questions.methodNote: Page 14 defines a rectangle by its four right angles and establishes that its opposite sides are equal. Page 3 models proving quadrilateral properties by triangle congruence and then using matching sides. The assigned question explicitly requests the alternative congruence proof, so its solution uses SAS rather than the Pythagoras proof on page 14.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: For the explicitly named triangles, select equal opposite sides, the common side and included right angles to establish SAS congruence, then use corresponding sides to conclude that the diagonals are equal.

classification.difficultyReason: Connect the circumradius to half a diagonal, then calculate the diagonal using Pythagoras’ theorem.

questions.mappingNote: Calculating a diagonal by Pythagoras is the most advanced directly assessed calculation; the diagonal properties identify that half its length is the required radius.
questions.methodNote: Page 14 calculates rectangle diagonals using Pythagoras’ theorem and states that diagonals are equal and bisect each other. Page 15 extends these properties to squares. Page 16 defines the circumcircle with its centre at the diagonal intersection. Pages 2–3 establish the underlying diagonal properties.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Connect the circumradius to half a diagonal, then calculate the diagonal using Pythagoras’ theorem.

classification.difficultyReason: Use equal sides and equal diagonals to establish four congruent triangles, then deduce four right angles.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed task is a proof that given side and diagonal properties force a quadrilateral to be a square. Proving properties of triangles and quadrilaterals is the closest supplied skill; triangle congruence is the supporting method.
questions.methodNote: Pages 9–10 demonstrate SSS congruence and conclusions from matching angles. Page 14 defines a rectangle by four right angles; page 15 defines a square as a rectangle with all sides equal. Use the four-triangle SSS argument indicated by the prepared answer, followed by the quadrilateral angle sum.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use equal sides and equal diagonals to establish four congruent triangles, then deduce four right angles.

classification.difficultyReason: Establish triangle congruence using perpendicular lines, then generalise the result to arbitrary perpendicular intervals by translation.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed method is constructing a congruence proof and extending it geometrically. The selected congruence-proof skill is the closest catalogue match. Part b retains its own complete conditions rather than receiving an invented shared stem.
questions.methodNote: Pages 3, 9 and 10 demonstrate congruence proofs using angle facts and matching sides. Pages 14–16 establish rectangle and square properties; page 15 supplies equal sides and right angles for a square. Use complementary angles and AAS for part a, then length-preserving translations for part b, as indicated by the prepared answer.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Establish triangle congruence using perpendicular lines, then generalise the result to arbitrary perpendicular intervals by translation.

classification.difficultyReason: Recall the taught diagonal properties of four named special quadrilaterals.

questions.mappingNote: The question directly assesses description of diagonal properties, so quadrilateral-properties is the closest catalogue skill. No proof or numerical unknown is requested.
questions.methodNote: Recall the established diagonal theorems. Parallelogram diagonals bisect each other; rhombus diagonals additionally meet perpendicularly and bisect vertex angles; rectangle diagonals additionally have equal lengths; squares inherit both sets of properties.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recall the taught diagonal properties of four named special quadrilaterals.

classification.difficultyReason: Select taught rhombus diagonal and angle-bisector facts, link with triangle/straight/co-interior angles and recognise equal radii plus parallel pairs; the stem explicitly supplies the intended property family.

questions.mappingNote: Part a directly uses the diagonal results on page 10. Part b combines those results with a straight angle and supplementary adjacent angles. Part c uses equal radii and the rhombus definition on page 9 before applying the diagonal angle-bisector property.
questions.methodNote: Use the definition of a rhombus, its parallelogram properties, perpendicular diagonals and diagonals that bisect interior angles; combine these with triangle angle sums and parallel-line angle facts.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select the stated rhombus diagonal properties and link them with triangle and supplementary angle sums; the circle supplies equal radii, while the stem already signals rhombus reasoning.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine rectangle and square diagonal properties with triangle, straight-line and parallel-line angle reasoning.

questions.mappingNote: Part a directly follows Example 4; part b applies square diagonal properties; part c combines equal half-diagonals with angle reasoning; part d uses alternate angles and a straight angle. The closest primary catalogue skill assesses unknown sides and angles in figures.
questions.methodNote: Page 14 establishes equal, bisecting rectangle diagonals. Page 15 Example 4 uses equal half-diagonals directly and states perpendicular, angle-bisecting square diagonals. Use these properties with isosceles triangles, triangle angle sums, parallel-line angles and straight angles.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine rectangle and square diagonal properties with triangle, straight-line and parallel-line angle reasoning.

classification.difficultyReason: Reconstruct the chapter's explicitly identified review proofs, introducing diagonals and linking parallel-line angles to triangle congruence; the final proof reuses the opposite-side result.

questions.mappingNote: All three parts require proofs of parallelogram properties, directly matching prove-properties-triangles-quadrilaterals. The solutions use the page 3 proof sequence and explicitly establish both opposite pairs and both diagonal halves.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 defines a parallelogram by parallel opposite sides. Page 3 proves opposite-angle equality using co-interior angles, opposite-side equality using diagonal AC and AAS, and diagonal bisection using AAS for ABM and CDM.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Reconstruct the chapter's explicitly identified review proofs, introducing diagonals and linking parallel-line angles to triangle congruence; the final proof reuses the opposite-side result.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct proofs of both rhombus diagonal properties using equal sides, parallel lines and triangle angle sums.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts require proofs of rhombus properties rather than merely recalling them, so proving properties of triangles and quadrilaterals is the primary skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 9 establishes a rhombus as a parallelogram. Page 10 proves diagonal angle bisection using equal-side triangles and perpendicularity using angle bisection and triangle angle sums; the prepared Review answer also uses alternate angles and isosceles base angles.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct proofs of both rhombus diagonal properties using equal sides, parallel lines and triangle angle sums.

classification.difficultyReason: Prove a general diagonal property by applying Pythagoras’ theorem to two right triangles.

questions.mappingNote: The task asks for a general proof of a rectangle property; proving properties of triangles and quadrilaterals is the closest directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 14 explicitly proves equality of rectangle diagonals using opposite-side equality and Pythagoras’ theorem in triangles ABC and BCD. The solution follows that sequence.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Prove a general diagonal property by applying Pythagoras’ theorem to two right triangles.

classification.difficultyReason: The four explicit prompts scaffold two similar SAS proofs and their alternate-angle consequences; students must connect these results to the definition of a parallelogram.

questions.mappingNote: The complete question establishes the diagonal-bisection test for a parallelogram through four scaffolded parts.
questions.methodNote: Use the given bisections and vertically opposite angles for SAS; infer matching angles, then use equal alternate angles to prove parallel sides. Page 2 supplies the parallelogram definition; pages 3 and 9 model congruence proofs followed by parallel-side conclusions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: The four explicit prompts scaffold two similar SAS proofs and their alternate-angle consequences; students must connect these results to the definition of a parallelogram.

classification.difficultyReason: Two explicit parts guide a SAS proof and its side-equality consequence; students must select diagonal bisection and combine adjacent and opposite side equalities.

questions.mappingNote: The two scaffolded parts prove the perpendicular-diagonals test for a rhombus. The converse property on page 10 is context, not a premise for this proof.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 supplies diagonal bisection and opposite-side equality in a parallelogram; page 9 defines a rhombus by four equal sides. Use bisection, the given right angles and the common side for SAS, then matching sides and opposite-side equalities.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Two explicit parts guide a SAS proof and its side-equality consequence; students must select diagonal bisection and combine adjacent and opposite side equalities.

classification.difficultyReason: The named triangles scaffold the SSS proof; the student must then select corresponding angles and use converse alternate-angle reasoning to establish both pairs of parallel sides.

questions.mappingNote: The question uses the page 9 method with diagonal BD and the printed correspondence ADB to CBD. Proving both pairs of opposite sides parallel establishes the final quadrilateral classification.
questions.methodNote: Page 9 proves that a rhombus is a parallelogram by joining a diagonal, applying SSS, and using matching angles and converse alternate-angle reasoning. Page 2 defines a parallelogram. Pages 3 and 10 demonstrate congruence proofs and conclusions from matching elements.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: The named triangles scaffold the SSS proof; the student must then select corresponding angles and use converse alternate-angle reasoning to establish both pairs of parallel sides.

classification.difficultyReason: Uses SSS congruence and supplementary equal angles to establish a rectangle test.

questions.mappingNote: The question proves a rectangle criterion through triangle congruence; the properties-proof skill is the closest supplied catalogue match.
questions.methodNote: Use equal opposite sides, SSS congruence, matching angles, co-interior angles and the definition of a rectangle.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Uses SSS congruence and supplementary equal angles to establish a rectangle test.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct the unstated extended configuration, select triangles PBQ and PCD, establish congruence using midpoint and angle relationships, and combine corresponding sides with segment addition.

questions.mappingNote: Triangle congruence is the principal directly assessed method for proving the doubled length.
questions.methodNote: Use vertically opposite and alternate angles with the midpoint equality to prove AAS congruence, then apply equal opposite sides and segment addition.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct the unstated extended configuration, select triangles PBQ and PCD, establish congruence using midpoint and angle relationships, and combine corresponding sides with segment addition.
